items.source: Substack Notes digest — Jeff Park / Michael Howell / BowTied Bull
items.title: Jeff Park: Google IPO'd at 1.5% of tech market cap. Anthropic IPOs at ~8%
items.idea: Jeff Park points out that Google was 1.5% of the tech sector's market cap when it listed in 2004. Anthropic is about 8% of the tech sector at its 2026 IPO. That is roughly 5x the relative weight at listing, so public investors are buying a company that is already huge, not a young one.
items.angle: Relative weight at IPO is a proxy for how much upside is left for public buyers. It also ties in with Parekh's note that Anthropic already trades below its $83 IPO price.
items.tweetA: Google listed at 1.5% of tech market cap. Anthropic listed at ~8%. Public markets didn't get the early growth this time. Private capital kept it, and retail is buying in near the top of the S-curve.
items.tweetB: Here's the uncomfortable math: if Anthropic is 8% of tech at IPO and already below its $83 issue price, the index funds that have to own it are the exit liquidity. Watch where index inclusion lands.

items.source: Substack Notes digest — Jeff Park / Michael Howell / BowTied Bull
items.title: Michael Howell: falling global liquidity explains the sell-off. 2027 upturn, but 'more bad news first'
items.idea: Michael Howell (CrossBorder Capital) blames the latest sell-off on a falling Global Liquidity cycle. He says 2026 asset allocation is 'on track' and that 2027 could bring a favourable upturn. His line is that 'we may need more bad news in order to feel good again': liquidity only turns after the stress forces policy to respond.
items.angle: This liquidity-cycle view clashes with Innes/Authers, who argue the Fed has no reason to rescue anything while GDP runs at 4.2%. Bad news is what reconciles the two.
items.tweetA: Howell says liquidity is still falling and the turn is a 2027 story. The Fed is pricing 2+ more hikes. So the bull case for next year needs something to break first. Pick your poison.
items.tweetB: The liquidity people and the macro people agree on the destination and disagree on the route. Howell: bad news makes the bottom. Authers: 4.2% GDP means no rescue. Both say the same thing for the next 3 months: don't chase.

items.source: Substack Notes digest — Jeff Park / Michael Howell / BowTied Bull
items.title: BowTied Bull: expect a Mike Tyson punch the moment you feel euphoria
items.idea: BowTied Bull's note: whether you're at $1M or $100M, 'the second you feel euphoria there will be a massive unknown punch coming at 70,000 mph'. It's a risk-management rule, not a market call. It was posted 7 days ago, before the Jensen-return squeeze.
items.angle: This works as a reflexivity reminder for the current tape, where euphoria 'all came back in a single day' on Monday (his own words in today's post) and then reversed on Tuesday.
items.tweetA: Monday: Jensen is back, euphoria returns in one session. Tuesday: deep red, closing at the lows. Nothing illustrates the 'punch when you feel euphoric' rule better than a single-day sentiment round-trip.
items.tweetB: The portfolio rule I keep relearning is to cut size when you feel smart, not when you feel scared. The feeling is the signal, and it's early every time.

items.source: AI Ramblings Daily ARD #215 / Michael Parekh
items.title: OpenAI's IPO clock: $10B Q3 revenue vs Anthropic's $17B, and a $750B compute bill through 2030
items.idea: Per the WSJ, OpenAI's Q3 revenue grew ~50% to $10B, while Anthropic reached $17B with a smaller operating loss. OpenAI plans ~$750B of compute spend through 2030, and a public listing gives it the tools to raise that. Anthropic's shares slipped below their $83 IPO price this week. Parekh's bar is that OpenAI must sustain a valuation above $1T to count as even a moderately successful IPO.
items.angle: The IPO-window argument is the real catalyst. Windows shut for years after 1987, the dot-com bust and the GFC, so OpenAI has an incentive to hurry while Anthropic's broken IPO sets the comp.
items.tweetA: OpenAI: $10B a quarter in revenue, $750B of compute commitments through 2030. That's ~19 years of current revenue already spent. The IPO isn't a liquidity event. It's a financing requirement.
items.tweetB: Anthropic trades below its $83 IPO price, and OpenAI needs $1T+ to call its IPO a success. The last mega-IPO always prices the cycle. If the window shuts like 2000 or 2008, the compute contracts don't disappear. The counterparties eat them.

items.title: Nvidia as the 'central bank of the AI boom': $100B+ in equity stakes, a $105B OpenAI lease backstop
items.idea: A WSJ tally has Nvidia holding over $100B of equity stakes in customers and suppliers, plus a $105B backstop on an OpenAI data-center lease in Ohio. Interim CEO Colette Kress sounded cautious on those deals, and Jensen's return could remove that caution. Nvidia's stock soared on Monday while its most actively traded bonds slipped.
items.angle: Stock up, bonds down on the same news is a textbook signal of equity holders gaining at creditors' expense (more risk-taking). It's worth watching NVDA CDS and bond spreads.
items.tweetA: When $NVDA stock rips and its bonds sell off on the same headline, the market is telling you who pays for the next round of vendor financing. $205B of stakes and lease backstops is a balance sheet, not a chip company.
items.tweetB: A $105B backstop on a single OpenAI lease in Ohio. For context, that's bigger than most investment-grade issuers' entire debt stacks. The kingmaker is now the lender of last resort.

In Shenzhen's electronics markets, servers with Nvidia's top chips are still on offer at sharply higher prices (WaPo).

items.tweetA: The remote-access rule did what export controls never did: it created a used-GPU supply glut in the US while Shenzhen pays a premium. The H100-backed loans assumed rental rates, not liquidation value. $CRWV
items.tweetB: Here's the spread to watch now: US secondary-market GPU price vs Shenzhen grey-market price. The wider it gets, the more smuggling pays, and the more Washington tightens again.

items.title: Fed vice chair: AI-related debt tops $800B this year, with off-balance-sheet commitments >3x that
items.idea: Per the WSJ, the Fed's vice chair for supervision puts AI-related debt on track to top $800B this year, with off-balance-sheet commitments tied to the buildout estimated at more than 3x that (i.e. >$2.4T). NY Fed's Williams: 'My big focus is... how strong this demand is, and much of it's related to AI.' Some officials see a slower AI buildout as part of slowing the economy, so a tech sell-off may not bother them.
items.angle: This is the key insight: the Fed sees AI capex as the inflation source. A tech correction is the policy working, not a reason to ease. The Fed put is struck far lower.
items.tweetA: $800B of on-balance-sheet AI debt and $2.4T+ off balance sheet, per the Fed's own supervisor. And the Fed sees AI demand as the inflation problem. You don't get a rescue when you ARE the reason for the hikes.
items.tweetB: Williams just told you the Fed's view: AI capex is the demand shock. That flips the 2022 playbook. Back then, tech sold off because of hikes. Now hikes happen partly to sell off tech capex. $QQQ $SMH

items.title: New tariff round: Yale Budget Lab sees the effective US tariff rate going from 11.4% to 13.9%
items.idea: A new tariff round against China, the EU, India and others was announced on Wednesday, the same week a key inflation measure hit a 3-year high (WSJ: 'Why This Is a Terrible Time for New Tariffs'). Yale's Budget Lab estimates it lifts the average effective US tariff from 11.4% to 13.9%, a +2.5pp jump.
items.angle: The tariff hike lands on core PCE at 3.3% with a Fed already hiking. That's a stagflation-tilted policy mix. Note that the prior Innes tariff piece (09:02 CEST, outside window) argued the inflation damage is modest.
items.tweetA: Effective tariff rate: 11.4% to 13.9%. Core PCE: 3.3% and rising. Fed: hiking in December. Every lever of policy is pulling in the same direction, and none of them is pointed at growth.
items.tweetB: +2.5pp on the effective tariff rate is roughly a 0.3-0.4pp one-time price-level bump on goods. Small on its own. But the Fed is hiking into a 'temporary' shock again. That's how 'transitory' becomes 'embedded'.

items.tweetB: 2021 was used cars. 2026 is used iPhones. Whenever a chip shortage hits a consumer good, the secondary market becomes the real price-discovery venue. Refurb is the underrated AI trade.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom — When the Machines Take Over (GS)
items.title: Goldman (Pasquariello): fast money has capitulated, but the machines run on a different clock
items.idea: Goldman's Tony Pasquariello sees some genuine capitulation among fast-money investors, but trend-followers and vol-control funds have been operating 'on an entirely different timetable'. Innes says the point at which systematic funds stop selling may matter more than the amount they have already liquidated. Once that happens, additional downside generates little incremental selling, while a strong rally forces them to rebuild exposure.
items.angle: Asymmetry depends on CTA trigger levels, not on fundamentals. Track the GS CTA flow estimates for the flat-tape and up-tape scenarios. Pairs with the SixSigma April-2025 analog.
items.tweetA: Discretionary hedge funds are done selling. CTAs aren't. The difference matters: humans capitulate on pain, models capitulate on trigger levels. Until the trend signals flip, every rally is supply. $SPY
items.tweetB: The asymmetry trade isn't 'buy the dip.' It's that the sellers left are mechanical and the buyers are optional. Once the models are flat, a +3% day forces them back in. That's the setup for a violent squeeze into year-end.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom — When the Machines Take Over (GS)
items.title: Three-way split: discretionary investors vs quant models vs retail buyers on whether the correction is over
items.idea: Innes highlights an emerging disagreement beneath the index swings. Discretionary investors see capitulation, quant projections are 'not quite ready to declare the coast clear', and retail keeps buying. 'Arguing with the machines about fundamentals is generally a rather expensive waste of time.'
items.angle: When retail is the only consistent dip buyer, the bottom depends on retail's staying power. That links to the Adler/Fear & Greed data and the BTC flows.
items.tweetA: Fast money capitulated. Retail bought. Quants are still selling. Three groups, three different clocks. The market bottoms when the slowest clock stops, and that's the machines.
items.tweetB: Hot take: retail buying every dip is not the bullish signal people think. It means the marginal seller hasn't been forced out yet, it's just been absorbed. Real bottoms usually see retail give up too.

items.source: The Founders Corner / Chris Tottman
items.title: ICE scoring: the CEO's AI feature has the highest impact and still finishes second from last
items.idea: In a worked example, six features are scored on Impact × Confidence × Ease. Bulk import scores 7×8×8 = 448, while 'AI route optimisation', the CEO's favourite with the top Impact of 9, scores 9×3×2 = 54 because confidence and ease are terrible. Switching to RICE (adding Reach) flips the top spot: ETA texts reach 300 accounts and score 420 vs bulk import's 112. 'Reach only means something once you've said what you're reaching for.'
items.angle: This is a useful lens on enterprise AI adoption: lots of AI features score high on Impact and terribly on Confidence × Ease. That's why AI revenue lags AI capex.
items.tweetA: Score the CEO's AI feature honestly: impact 9, confidence 3, ease 2 = 54. Boring bulk import = 448. That's the enterprise AI adoption gap in one multiplication.
items.tweetB: Multiplicative scoring is brutal: one honest 2 kills a 9. Now apply it to AI capex: impact 10, confidence in ROI maybe 3, ease (power, memory, credit) 2. The market is doing this math right now.

items.source: The Founders Corner / Chris Tottman
items.title: Kohavi/Microsoft: 1/3 of vetted ideas help, 1/3 do nothing, 1/3 hurt. Booking: 9 in 10 fail
items.idea: Ronny Kohavi's Microsoft experiments showed that ideas which had already passed every internal bar split roughly into thirds: improved, neutral, worse (Bing's success rate was lower). Stefan Thomke (HBS) reports ~90% of Booking.com ideas fail to move their target metric. Pendo's 2019 report across 615 products: ~12% of features drive 80% of daily usage, and 80% of features are rarely or never used. 'A Confidence score of 8 on an untested idea isn't optimism. It's a statistical error.'
items.angle: This is a base-rate argument for AI product roadmaps and for investment theses alike: most 'conviction' ideas don't work. Size accordingly.
items.tweetA: Microsoft's own data: of ideas that passed every internal review, a third made things worse. Booking.com: 90% fail. Now think about how many AI agent features are shipping with zero A/B tests.
items.tweetB: 12% of software features drive 80% of usage (Pendo, 615 products). If AI copilots follow the same power law, most of the per-seat AI upsell is shelfware, and renewals will show it. $CRM $NOW $MSFT

items.source: The Hard Fork / Marvin Liao
items.title: '3 years to avoid the permanent underclass': the salary model ends, so convert time into scarce assets
items.idea: Marvin Liao amplifies a viral thesis (@yerocode) that human work has 'a maximum of 3 years' of real earning power left before automation makes most salaried work not worth paying for. That would end the 200-year 'rent your time for 40 years' model. Prescription: convert salary into non-automatable assets (Bitcoin, land, energy, compute, distribution, food production). Liao half-endorses it: 'I don't know if I completely buy into this. But maybe better safe than sorry.'
items.angle: The meme itself is the signal. It's a cultural driver of the household bid for scarce assets (BTC, gold, land) and a labor-anxiety indicator that could show up in savings rates and political demand for redistribution.
items.tweetA: The '3 years before the permanent underclass' meme is everywhere. Whether or not it's right, a generation acting on it is a structural bid for $BTC, land and compute, funded out of consumption. That's the macro effect.
items.tweetB: If labor's share really collapses in 3 years, the trade isn't just 'own assets'. It's that governments will tax the assets. Every 'convert labor into capital' thesis ignores that capital is where the next tax base moves.

items.title: Q3 real GDP at 4.2% annualized, and supercore PCE still above comfort: 'too hot for a rescue'
items.idea: Q3 real GDP came in at ~4.2% annualized, exceptionally strong outside the pandemic swings. The Fed's preferred underlying services measure (supercore ex-housing) remains above comfort and isn't just an energy pass-through. Carl Weinberg (HFE): the economy has enough momentum to absorb more rate increases. 'An economy growing above 4% makes it rather difficult to argue that monetary policy has already become intolerably restrictive.'
items.angle: The strong-GDP plus sticky-supercore mix pushes the Fed put far below current levels. Tech's problem is valuation and liquidity, not the economy.
items.tweetA: 4.2% real GDP. Supercore above target. Core PCE 3.3%. Anyone asking for a Fed rescue is asking a central bank to ease into a boom because Nasdaq is down 15%. That's not happening.
items.tweetB: Here's the irony: AI capex is a big part of why GDP is at 4.2%, and it's the reason the Fed won't save AI stocks. The boom is too strong for its own good.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom — Groundhog Thanksgiving (Authers)
items.title: Robin Brooks: the Fed is tightening into falling oil, so rising real rates mean policy-error risk
items.idea: Robin Brooks (Brookings) warns that the Fed is tightening into falling oil prices, pushing real interest rates higher and increasing the risk of a policy error. With the blackout period approaching, officials have little chance to reassure markets before December. His concern: continued liquidation could become severe enough to force a reassessment. The counterpoint: Wednesday's cross-asset reversal undermines the systemic-crisis narrative.
items.angle: Falling oil plus rising nominal rates means real rates are spiking. That's historically worse for gold and long-duration assets, yet gold held $3,500+.
items.tweetA: Oil falling, Fed hiking. Real rates rising from both ends. Brooks calls it policy error risk. I call it the setup where the Fed breaks something it can't see from the dashboard. And the blackout means no backpedaling until Dec 9.
items.tweetB: If real rates are rising this fast and gold still holds $3,500+, gold isn't trading real rates anymore. It's trading fiscal and Fed-credibility risk. Different driver, different hedge. $GLD

items.title: Wednesday's 4-asset reversal: gold $3,425 to $3,575+, 10y 4.80% to 4.86%, BTC closes higher
items.idea: During Wednesday's session, gold fell toward $3,425 before recovering above $3,575. Bitcoin followed a similarly violent path and finished higher. Global equities recovered most of their losses, and the 10y Treasury yield went from 4.80% (flight to safety) back to 4.86%. Innes: in a leveraged liquidation, gold falls alongside tech because traders need cash, and the reversal is equally mechanical once the selling programme finishes.
items.angle: A 4.4% intraday gold range is a liquidation signature, not a fundamental move. Gold behaving as a source of cash means it gets sold first in a margin call and bought first after.
items.tweetA: Gold: $3,425 to $3,575 intraday, a 4.4% range in one session. When the safe haven swings like a meme stock, it's being used as an ATM for margin calls. That's a bottoming tell, not a top. $GLD $GC
items.tweetB: Gold, BTC, equities and the 10y all reversed on the same afternoon. When every asset class moves together, it's one trade: deleveraging. The question isn't which asset bottomed. It's whether the leverage is gone.

items.title: Jensen came back, the market didn't: NVDA still ~20% below its early-October high, SOX -17%

The issues extend beyond management: hyperscaler capex sustainability, financing structures, and whether returns justify the commitments. 'An unexpected corporate development can force short sellers to cover. It cannot automatically restore confidence in the economics of a multi-year investment cycle.'
items.angle: The CEO-return catalyst is spent. The next catalyst is earnings season (~2 months out) or the Fed. Until then, semis trade on flows.
items.tweetA: $NVDA got its CEO back and is still -20% from October. That's how you know it was never about Jensen. It's about who pays for $750B of OpenAI compute and $105B lease backstops at 5% rates.
items.tweetB: Short covering lasted exactly one session. That's the market telling you the governance discount was the small one. The cost-of-capital discount is the big one, and it hasn't moved. $SMH

items.title: The defining trade of the ChatGPT era (long QQQ / short TLT) has broken trend for a third time
items.idea: Since ChatGPT's launch, owning tech while staying short duration has been one of the most persistent cross-asset trends. The QQQ/TLT ratio has now had its third major interruption, after Liberation Day and the Iran conflict. Both earlier breaks recovered, but this time Jensen's return failed to restore the trend. With the 10y having topped 5.25% in September, the market may be reconsidering the cost of capital and the return on capital at the same time.
items.angle: If QQQ/TLT doesn't reclaim its trend, the regime change is from 'growth beats rates' to 'rates bite growth'. That favours a barbell of duration and value over long tech/short bonds.
items.tweetA: Long $QQQ / short $TLT made money for four years straight. It broke at Liberation Day and recovered. It broke in the Iran conflict and recovered. It's broken now, and the Jensen catalyst didn't fix it. Third time is the one to respect.
items.tweetB: When the most crowded cross-asset trade of a cycle breaks, it doesn't just hit tech. It hits every risk-parity and vol-target book that assumed stocks and bonds stay negatively correlated. That's the real liquidity story.

items.title: In earnings we trust: NDX 2026/2027 EPS estimates still rising while prices fall

The gap between trailing and forward P/E is widening, which looks cheap if forecasts hold and offers little protection if they're revised. The next earnings season is ~2 months away, a long gap for expectations to shift without confirmation.
items.angle: This is a two-month window with no hard data. Watch preannouncements, hyperscaler capex commentary at conferences, and sell-side revisions breadth. The first wave of cuts is the real signal.
items.tweetA: Price down 15%, 2027 EPS estimates up. Either this is the best entry since April 2025, or analysts are the last to know. With two months to earnings season, revisions breadth is the only number that matters.
items.tweetB: Cheap on forward P/E is the most dangerous phrase in a capex cycle. In 2000 and 2022, forward multiples looked fine right up until the E got cut. Watch the hyperscaler capex guides, not the multiples. $QQQ

items.title: Bowers: the Fed put has a higher strike than investors think (dot-com, not 2008)
items.idea: David Bowers (Absolute Strategy) argues that strong profits and margins are not disinflationary, so the Fed has little reason to abandon its mandate because tech fell. The Fed kept tightening early in the dot-com collapse because it didn't threaten the wider economy, while 2008 forced action because it hit banks and funding markets. The AI correction hasn't shown systemic damage yet. Chris Watling (Longview) is more constructive: he sees a mid-cycle correction, with a resolute Fed anchoring expectations and allowing yields to fall, but considerable sideways volatility.
items.angle: The policy trigger is credit and funding markets, not equity drawdowns. Watch IG spreads, neocloud bonds and repo, not the Nasdaq.
items.tweetA: The Fed didn't rescue dot-com stocks until the economy cracked. It rescued 2008 because banks cracked. The AI correction hasn't touched either yet. So the Fed put isn't at -15% on $QQQ. It's at the first neocloud default.
items.tweetB: Watling says mid-cycle correction plus sideways chop. Bowers says no Fed put. Both mean the same thing for positioning: sell rallies in the most levered AI names and wait for credit to tell you when it's over.

items.title: BTC Fear & Greed at 11, its 14th straight day in Extreme Fear, while US stocks drop to 12
items.idea: Sentiment indices for US stocks, the Nasdaq and Bitcoin all remain in Extreme Fear. US stocks fell from 15 to 12 on the day, the Nasdaq held at 15, and Bitcoin dropped from 13 to 11 on November 26, its 14th straight day in Extreme Fear. Adler's paid section looks at holder selling pressure and how close the market is to the zone where sellers typically exhaust, plus the 30- and 90-day forward returns from similar episodes since 2016.
items.angle: Fourteen days of extreme fear while BTC is +1% today ($60.8K per Rosenberg) is the classic divergence where sentiment lags price.
items.tweetA: Bitcoin Fear & Greed: 11. Fourteen days straight in Extreme Fear. And BTC is up 1% today while the US is closed. Sentiment this washed out with price stabilizing is usually where the asymmetry is. $BTC
items.tweetB: US stocks at 12, Nasdaq at 15, Bitcoin at 11. When every fear gauge sits below 15 at the same time, it's not an asset-specific story. It's cross-asset deleveraging, and those end with a flow, not a headline.

items.title: October PCE: 3.8% headline, core accelerates to 3.3% vs 3.2% expected, and real spending is negative
items.idea: Headline PCE was 3.8% y/y in October. Core picked up from 3.1% to 3.3% y/y, above the 3.2% forecast, strengthening the case for a December hike. Core PCE rose 0.3% m/m, the same as September. Real consumer spending fell by less than 0.1%.
items.angle: Accelerating core plus slightly negative real spending is the stagflation signature, hidden inside a 4.2% Q3 GDP print that is already backward-looking.
items.tweetA: Core PCE: 3.1% to 3.3%, above consensus. Real spending: negative. Q3 GDP of 4.2% is the rear-view mirror. October is what Q4 looks like: prices up, volumes down. That's not a soft landing. $TLT
items.tweetB: 0.3% m/m core for two straight months annualizes to ~3.7%. The Fed's target is 2%. Anyone pricing cuts in 2027 is betting on a recession, not a disinflation.
